names.name: Omamori
names.th: โอมาโมริ (เครื่องรางญี่ปุ่น)

etymology.root: Japanese mamori 守り 'protection', with the honorific prefix o- (sonkeigo) — 'the honoured protection'
etymology.note: The same character stands behind ofuda's shinsatsu vocabulary; omamori shares its origin with ofuda and is described as the smaller, portable version of it.

text.what: A small brocade pouch, a few centimetres tall, drawn shut at the top with a cord and printed with the name of the shrine or temple that issued it. Inside is a slip of paper or a chip of wood carrying a prayer or an invocation. The pouch stays shut: nobody who carries one opens it. Most hang from a bag, a school satchel, a phone strap or a car mirror rather than round the neck.
text.story:
Omamori are issued by Shinto shrines and by Buddhist temples alike, dedicated to particular kami or to Buddhist figures, and sold to anyone regardless of what they believe. The shrine consecrates the contents by rite; a Shinto one is described as holding busshin, spiritual offshoots of the deity, a Buddhist one kesshin, manifestations.

The folklorist Yanagita Kunio dated the thing a reader now recognises to the Tokugawa period at the earliest. Writing in 1969 he put it this way: "Japanese have probably always believed in amulets of one kind or another, but the modern printed charms now given out by shrines and temples first became popular in the Tokugawa period or later, and the practice of a person wearing miniature charms is also new. The latter custom is particularly common in cities." Two claims sit in that sentence — the printed charm is early modern, the pocket-sized charm is later still, and urban.

The demand outgrew the shrines. Where a popular shrine or temple cannot keep up, it orders omamori from a factory, and priests have objected to the quality and to what they call the "authenticity" of the factory product. Both halves of that get reported here: the factory pouch and the hand-finished one come off the same counter, and the argument over whether they are the same object is an argument inside the tradition.

*Inference —* a charm designed to be replaced every twelve months is a charm with a business model, and the New Year crowds are the year's trade. Fushimi Inari-taisha alone drew 2.69 million worshippers over three days at the New Year in 2006, a police figure and the largest in western Japan. No source this project has read publishes what any shrine takes in omamori money, so no figure is given here.
text.how: Received, not bought — the verb the tradition uses is sazukaru, to be granted, and the money handed over is hatsuhoryō, a first-fruit offering. If a visitor cannot find one for their need, they may ask a priest to have one made; if enough people ask for the same one, the shrine starts stocking it. The pouch is then carried, tied to a bag or a strap, and not opened; opening it loses what is in it. It is customarily swapped for a new one once a year. The old one goes back to the shrine or temple it came from, usually on or just after New Year, and is burnt rather than thrown out, at the Sagichō or Dondoyaki fire held at the Little New Year on 14 or 15 January. Most Shinto shrines will accept another shrine's omamori; many will not accept a Buddhist one, and the reverse holds too.
text.today: Still issued by nearly every shrine and temple in Japan as of 2026, in a spread of categories a buyer picks from: kōtsū-anzen for the road, gakugyō-jōju for exams, shōbai-hanjō for trade, en-musubi for finding a partner, anzan for a safe delivery, kanai-anzen for the household, yaku-yoke against a bad year. Alongside them, shops sell omamori-shaped goods with Mickey Mouse, Hello Kitty, Snoopy or Kewpie on them, issued by no shrine and consecrated by nobody — a separate product that borrows the shape.

text_th.what: ถุงผ้าไหมยกดอกใบเล็ก สูงไม่กี่เซนติเมตร รูดปิดด้านบนด้วยเชือก และพิมพ์ชื่อศาลเจ้าหรือวัดที่ออกให้ ข้างในเป็นแผ่นกระดาษหรือชิ้นไม้ที่มีคำอธิษฐานหรือคำวิงวอน ถุงต้องปิดไว้เสมอ ไม่มีใครที่พกโอมาโมริเปิดมันออก ส่วนใหญ่แขวนไว้กับกระเป๋า กระเป๋านักเรียน สายห้อยโทรศัพท์ หรือกระจกรถ มากกว่าห้อยคอ

dating.label: c. 1603 to now, for the printed charm; the pouch worn on a person is later
dating.note: Dated from Yanagita Kunio's statement that the modern printed charms given out by shrines and temples became popular in the Tokugawa period or later. The start of that period, 1603, is used as the earliest year the statement can carry; it is not an attestation.

object.made_by: the shrine or temple, which consecrates the contents by rite; where demand outruns the counter, a factory makes the pouch
object.inscription: a prayer or invocation on the paper or wood inside, and the shrine's or temple's name on the outside
object.note: The pouch is not opened, so the contents are described from the tradition's own account rather than from an inspection. Modern issues have also been made as bumper decals, bicycle reflectors and card-shaped charms.

an omikuji is a loose paper strip with a graded fortune printed on it, drawn at random; an omamori is sewn shut and chosen by category
